classification.difficultyReason: Identify terms with the same pronumeral and combine their signed coefficients, keeping the two pronumeral groups separate.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c combine one set of like terms. Parts d–i separately collect the two pronumerals, retaining coefficient signs. The source margin explicitly refers to Example 1a. Neither offered reuse candidate matches this complete nine-part task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines like terms and Example 1a combines coefficients while retaining each pronumeral. Page 3 continues collecting like terms after expansion; expansion is not required here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients of like terms, including negative coefficients and two pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish terms by their complete variable factors and powers, combine signed coefficients, and recognise when opposite terms cancel.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c collect a single type of term as in Example 1b. Parts d and e distinguish unlike powers and collect each type as in Example 1c. Part f additionally cancels opposite xy terms. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete six-part source task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines like terms by identical pronumeral factors and powers. Example 1 combines their coefficients while retaining unlike terms separately. Page 3 continues collection after expansion; no expansion is needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of matching algebraic terms, distinguishing different powers and cancelling opposite terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the supplied distributive method to both bracket terms, controlling negative signs and simplifying numerical products, including fractions.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts require distribution across one bracket. Parts e–i and m–o require negative-sign control; j–o also require exact fraction multiplication. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states the distributive law a(b+c)=ab+ac. Example 2 multiplies each bracket term by the outside factor, including negative and algebraic factors. Page 3 continues distribution before collecting like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute positive, negative and fractional multipliers across two terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute a monomial across a binomial and simplify variable products into powers, retaining signs and unlike variable factors.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e use variable multipliers; f–g apply negative variable multipliers; h–l distribute products containing multiple pronumerals. These are direct applications of Example 2c, d. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete twelve-part task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 states the distributive law and Example 2c, d demonstrates variable multipliers and negative variable multipliers. Multiply the outside term by each bracket term, retaining signs and simplifying products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the distributive law to two terms, including variable and negative multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify distributive-law, sign and algebraic-product errors, explain each mistake and supply the correct expansion.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and h test applying the multiplier to every term; b and i test multiplying rather than adding numerical coefficients; c, d and g test product signs; e and f test multiplication of repeated pronumerals; j tests retaining both pronumeral factors. The supplied reuse candidates do not match this complete ten-part error-analysis task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces the distributive law a(b+c)=ab+ac. Example 2 distributes positive, negative and algebraic multipliers. Page 3 Examples 3 and 4 retain expanded products before collecting like terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify distributive-law, sign and algebraic-product errors, explain each mistake and supply the correct expansion.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute numerical and algebraic multipliers, including negative fractions, then collect like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c distribute a positive integer and collect constants; d–e collect linear terms; f–h distribute algebraic multipliers and collect like terms without combining different degrees; i cancels opposite linear terms; j combines fractional coefficients using sixths; k–l distribute negative fractional multipliers before collecting like terms. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete twelve-part source task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 recalls the distributive law and collecting like terms. Example 2 includes negative and algebraic multipliers. Page 3 Example 3 expands first and then collects like terms, retaining separate algebraic degrees.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute numerical and algebraic multipliers, including negative fractions, then collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand two brackets with signed numerical or variable multipliers, then identify and collect like terms, including complete cancellation of squared terms.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess distributive expansion followed by collection. Parts d, e, h and j require distributing a negative multiplier; parts f–j include pronumeral multipliers. Special-product methods on pages 4–5 are not needed.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 on PDF page 3 expands each bracket separately and then collects like terms. Example 3 supports pronumeral multipliers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand two bracketed terms, including negative and pronumeral multipliers, then collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Generate all four products from two binomials, track their signs, and combine the middle terms using the taught expansion procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Every part a–r is an ordinary binomial product directly matching Example 5, including signed constants and non-unit leading coefficients. The assigned reuse candidates concern different original tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 on pages 3–4 distributes each term of the first binomial over the second, expands the remaining brackets, then collects like terms. Page 5 treats difference-of-squares products separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand monic and non-monic binomial products, including negative terms, and collect like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand binomials containing two pronumerals and collect signed like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–i assesses a general binomial product with two pronumerals; expand-binomial-products is the directly assessed skill. The supplied reuse candidates contain different tasks and are incompatible.
questions.methodNote: Use the distributive expansion demonstrated in Example 5 on pages 3–4: multiply each term of the first binomial by the second binomial, expand, then collect like terms. Page 5's difference-of-squares method is not needed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand binomials containing two pronumerals and collect signed like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Match each binomial square to the sum or difference identity, square both complete terms, and form the signed double product.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts are binomial squares explicitly associated with Example 6. Parts a–d use the sum identity; parts e–i use the difference identity. Coefficients and two-pronumeral products follow Example 6c–d. The supplied reuse candidates describe different tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 develops (a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2 and (a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2. Example 6 substitutes the two terms, evaluates their squares and twice their product, then simplifies. Page 5 repeats these identities in the quadratic identities summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the square identities demonstrated in Example 6, including numerical coefficients and two pronumerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise conjugate factors and apply the taught difference-of-squares identity, correctly squaring coefficients and retaining the subtraction order.

questions.mappingNote: Every part of Question 11 is a conjugate binomial product matching Example 7 on page 5. The skill special-products directly assesses the identity used in all nine responses.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 demonstrates distributive expansion and collection of like terms; page 4 develops square identities. Page 5 derives the difference-of-two-squares identity, and Example 7 applies it by squaring each term and subtracting.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the difference-of-two-squares identity, including algebraic terms with numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and apply square and difference-of-squares identities with numerical and algebraic terms.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c, d and h use difference of two squares. Parts b, e, f, g and i use the sum or difference square identity. This directly assesses special products rather than general binomial multiplication.
questions.methodNote: Use the square identities demonstrated in Example 6 and the difference-of-squares identity demonstrated in Example 7; evaluate the squares and middle product exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and apply square and difference-of-squares identities with numerical and algebraic terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Select inverse operations or clear numerical denominators, then isolate the variable while maintaining equality and handling a negative coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use Example 8a's inverse operations, e–f use Example 8b's expansion, and g–j use Example 8c's denominator clearing. Part j directly assesses an equation containing multiple fractions, determining the primary skill. Pages 9, 10 and 12 were inspected as supplied context; their inequality and word-problem methods are not needed for this question.
questions.methodNote: Example 8a isolates the pronumeral by equal operations; Example 8b expands brackets before solving and simplifies fractional results; Example 8c multiplies both sides by the lowest common denominator. These methods are used without decimal approximation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Progresses from two-step equations to equations requiring a common denominator and division by a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand brackets on both sides, choose operations that gather variable terms and constants separately, and divide to obtain an exact solution.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d directly assess gathering pronumerals from both sides; parts e–h additionally require bracket expansion. The complete question therefore maps primarily to solving three-step linear equations.
questions.methodNote: Example 8d expands both brackets, gathers pronumerals on one side using equal operations on both sides, and isolates the pronumeral. Exact fractions are retained as in Example 8b.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Gather pronumerals from both sides, expanding brackets where necessary, and retain exact fractional solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Solve using inverse operations, reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative, and translate the result into the correct endpoint type and ray direction.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b use division by a positive coefficient; c–d use negative coefficients; e–f first undo an additive term; g–h combine undoing an additive term with negative division. Every part explicitly requires a number-line graph, so solving linear inequalities is primary and number-line representation is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 introduces inequality symbols and adding or subtracting the same number on both sides. Page 9 states that multiplication or division by a negative reverses the inequality sign; Example 9a–b demonstrates inverse operations and open or closed endpoints with solution rays. Pages 10 and 12 were inspected and concern word-problem modelling rather than the assessed inequality method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve one- and two-step inequalities, reversing the sign for negative multipliers or divisors, and graph each solution.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand and collect signed terms, gather variables from both sides where needed, and preserve or reverse the inequality according to the final operation.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess solving linear inequalities. Parts a–d collect pronumerals from both sides; e–j also expand brackets. Parts e, g, h and j explicitly apply division by a negative coefficient. The printed instruction asks only for solutions, so no number-line drawing is added.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 states that adding or subtracting the same number preserves an inequality. Page 9 adds the multiplication and division rules. Example 9c collects pronumerals, adjusts constants and divides; Example 9d expands brackets, collects terms and reverses the sign when dividing by a negative number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Solve inequalities with pronumerals on both sides, including bracket expansion and reversal when dividing by a negative coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the target average covers five tests, find the required total, and subtract the four known marks using the taught missing-mark model.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly follows Example 10’s missing-test-mark model. Finding a value from a given mean is the most specific assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 defines the fifth test mark as x, forms the mean as the total of five marks divided by five, simplifies the known marks, multiplies both sides by five and subtracts the known total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Form an equation for the mean of five test marks and solve for the missing mark.

classification.difficultyReason: Express length in terms of width, include both pairs of sides in a perimeter equation, solve it, and substitute back to report both dimensions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 uses the same rectangular-room perimeter model as Example 11, with length 2x+3 rather than x+3. Equation modelling is the primary assessed skill; finding dimensions from perimeter is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Example 11 on PDF page 10 defines the width as a pronumeral, expresses the length in terms of it, adds the four sides and solves the resulting linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the length in terms of the width, form a perimeter equation and solve for both dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Express two related numbers using one pronumeral and form an equation from their sum.

questions.mappingNote: The word-problem approach on page 10, particularly Example 11, supports expressing both numbers using one unknown; Example 8 on page 8 supplies the linear-equation method. Page 12 reinforces the same modelling sequence. Page 9 concerns inequalities and is not needed for this task.
questions.methodNote: Choose a pronumeral, express the related quantity in terms of it, form an equation from the given total, and solve by collecting like terms and applying the same operation to both sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express two related numbers using one pronumeral and form an equation from their sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Express three related shares using one pronumeral and form an equation for their total.

questions.mappingNote: The word-problem modelling in Examples 10 and 11 on page 10 supports setting C's share to x; the three shares total 540. Example 12 on page 12 reinforces expressing related quantities with one pronumeral. Equation solving follows Example 8 on page 8; the inequality methods on page 9 are not needed.
questions.methodNote: Choose a pronumeral for the required unknown quantity, express the related quantities using it, form an equation and solve by collecting like terms and dividing both sides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express three related shares using one pronumeral and form an equation for their total.

classification.difficultyReason: Express running speed in terms of walking speed and model the combined distance with a linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 applies the word-problem modelling approach on page 10 to walking and running distances; the directly assessed skill is constructing and solving the resulting linear equation.
questions.methodNote: Choose a pronumeral for the required unknown, express related quantities using it, form an equation and solve by equivalent operations. Page 12 Example 12 models travelled distances using speeds and elapsed time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express running speed in terms of walking speed and model the combined distance with a linear equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Express the renovation cost as a fraction of the unknown house price, then model and solve the total-cost equation.

questions.mappingNote: The word-problem modelling demonstrated in Examples 10 and 11 on page 10 applies directly: the house price is the unknown and the renovation cost is one sixth of it. Page 12 reinforces introducing an appropriate pronumeral. Inequality methods on page 9 are not required.
questions.methodNote: Choose a pronumeral for the requested unknown, express the related quantity in that pronumeral, form an equation and solve. Clear the numerical denominator by multiplying both sides, following Example 8c.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express the renovation cost as a fraction of the unknown house price, then model and solve the total-cost equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Express the two speeds with one variable and recognise that their distances over the shared hour add to the initial separation, then recover both speeds.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 uses the same towards-each-other model as Example 12, with cyclists 12 km apart and a speed difference of 2 km/h. Equation modelling is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 defines the slower traveller's speed with one pronumeral, expresses the faster speed by adding the difference, and adds the distances travelled in one hour to obtain a linear equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expresses two related speeds using one pronumeral and models the combined distance before solving.

classification.difficultyReason: Models both the increased acid volume and increased solution volume, then solves a linear equation with the unknown on both sides.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 has the same pure-acid addition structure as Example 13. The inspected beginning and continuation supply the complete taught method.
questions.methodNote: Following Example 13, introduce the added pure-acid volume, calculate the original acid volume, equate the new acid volume to the desired fraction of the increased total volume, expand and solve, then check the concentration.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Models both the increased acid volume and increased solution volume, then solves a linear equation with the unknown on both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: Express one coin count in terms of the other, then model the total value with a linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: The coin count gives 27-x coins of the other denomination. Equating their combined value to 2340 cents directly assesses modelling a word problem with a linear equation.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral for an unknown quantity, express the related quantity using it, translate the information into an equation, expand, collect terms and solve. Examples 12 and 13 demonstrate this modelling sequence; Example 8 supplies the linear-equation operations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express one coin count in terms of the other, then model the total value with a linear equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Express two complementary sales amounts using one variable and solve an equation combining different commission rates.

questions.mappingNote: The required first-company sales are x and the remaining sales are 7600-x. Adding the two percentage commissions gives the required earnings equation.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral for the required unknown, express related quantities in terms of it, translate the situation into an equation, expand and collect terms, then isolate the unknown. Example 14 converts commission percentages to decimal multipliers; Examples 12 and 13 demonstrate one-variable modelling.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express two complementary sales amounts using one variable and solve an equation combining different commission rates.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the linked operating times into one variable, sum two rate-times-time pollution contributions, impose the upper limit, and interpret its endpoint as both maximum times.

questions.mappingNote: Introduce the second operating time as t, express the first as 3t/2 + 2, and sum rate × time contributions. The phrase 'no more than' requires ≤. Solve the resulting inequality and substitute its upper endpoint to find both maximum times.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 explain solving linear inequalities by equivalent operations. Page 12 introduces a pronumeral for an unknown quantity and expresses related quantities using it. Example 14 on page 13 models a worded condition with a linear inequality and interprets its solution in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express related operating times using one variable, model the pollution limit with an inequality, and interpret the maximum for both smokestacks.

classification.difficultyReason: Model dilution by conserving the mass of salt while increasing the solution volume, then solve a linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 adapts Example 13 to dilution: added water increases total volume without changing salt mass. Forming and solving the concentration equation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 12–13, Example 13, introduce a pronumeral for added volume, express the final solution volume, equate the constituent amount calculated from concentration, and solve the resulting linear equation. Page 8 supplies linear-equation working; page 9 concerns inequalities and is not required for this equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model dilution by conserving the mass of salt while increasing the solution volume, then solve a linear equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Use overall average speed to obtain the total distance, then model the two journey legs with one unknown.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 requires modelling the two journey legs as x and x+30 after using overall average speed and the combined eight-hour journey to obtain their total distance. Equation modelling is the primary assessed skill; whole-journey average speed is a supporting skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 introduces an unknown quantity with a pronumeral and translates a travel problem into a linear equation in Example 12. Page 10 Example 11 expresses a second quantity in terms of the first and solves their total. Page 8 Example 8 supplies the inverse-operation equation-solving method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use overall average speed to obtain the total distance, then model the two journey legs with one unknown.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect annual revenue to occupied room-nights, then distinguish occupancy percentage from the proportions of occupied rooms charged each linked rate and construct a weighted revenue equation.

questions.mappingNote: Part a models annual revenue as occupied room-nights multiplied by the daily rate. Part b expresses the second rate as s+30 and combines the two percentage-weighted revenue contributions. Both use the equation-modelling method taught in this section. A 365-day year reproduces the supplied answers.
questions.methodNote: Choose a pronumeral for the required unknown, translate the practical conditions into a linear equation, expand and collect terms, then solve. Pages 12–13 demonstrate expressing related quantities in one pronumeral and modelling percentage quantities; page 10 demonstrates defining the unknown before forming an equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model annual room revenue using occupancy percentages, then form a linear equation for two related daily rates.

classification.difficultyReason: Model savings as a percentage of hourly earnings and solve a minimum-value inequality.

questions.mappingNote: The hourly earnings are 25.50h and savings are 0.25 times those earnings. 'At least' requires a non-strict lower bound. The source gives no whole-hour restriction.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral for the unknown quantity, translate the financial condition into an inequality, and divide both sides by the positive coefficient. Page 13 Example 14 models percentage earnings using a linear inequality; page 9 demonstrates solving inequalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model savings as a percentage of hourly earnings and solve a minimum-value inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent each pay offer as a function of the same sales amount, form a strict inequality, and interpret the solved threshold as sales that must be exceeded.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed task is forming and solving a linear inequality for weekly sales; commission calculations supply the context.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a pronumeral for the unknown quantity, express each payment algebraically, compare using a strict inequality, collect terms and divide by the positive coefficient. Example 14 models this same commission comparison.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model two commission arrangements and solve a strict inequality to determine when one pays more.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate a weighted examination total into an inequality, then substitute two marks and solve for the required examination mark.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task combines the weighted marks as x+2y, interprets 'at least' as greater than or equal to, and isolates y by subtraction and division by positive 2. Part b substitutes each supplied Term 1 mark without imposing an unstated whole-mark restriction.
questions.methodNote: Pages 8–9 teach preserving an inequality when adding or subtracting the same quantity and dividing by a positive number. Page 10 models examination marks algebraically. Pages 12–13 introduce pronumerals, translate practical conditions into algebra and solve; Example 14 demonstrates modelling a required condition with an inequality.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate a weighted examination total into an inequality, then substitute two marks and solve for the required examination mark.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution followed by multiplication and addition.

questions.mappingNote: The subject U is already isolated; the task assesses numerical substitution without rearrangement.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given values and evaluate using the order of operations, as in Example 15.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution followed by multiplication and addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute decimals into a bracketed fraction and evaluate in order.

questions.mappingNote: The subject s is already isolated, so numerical evaluation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute first, retaining the brackets and fraction, then evaluate; Examples 15 and 17 demonstrate substitution into grouped expressions and fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute decimals into a bracketed fraction and evaluate in order.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute four given values into a fractional formula and round to one decimal place.

questions.mappingNote: Direct formula substitution is primary; the question explicitly adds rounding to one decimal place.
